Trains are unable to use platforms 1 and 2 at Tattenham Corner due to a points failure. This means trains will be delayed arriving into and departing the station. You can use your normal route, but please allow extra time.

nrIncident.routes: between Streatham Hill and Norwood Junction
nrIncident.message:
A fault with the signalling system between Streatham Hill and Norwood Junction means fewer lines are able to run on the line towards Crystal Palace. As a result, some trains between these stations will be cancelled.
Disruption is expected until 11:45.
Customer advice:
Fewer trains than normal are able to run between Streatham Hill and Norwood Junction. This is due to a signal failure in the Crystal Palace area.
Services that normally run between London Victoria and West Croydon via Crystal Palace will divert via Streatham Common instead. This is only affecting South-bound trains. Trains towards London will run as booked.

Can you tell me more about the incident?
Track circuits are part of the signalling system and are used to detect where trains are on the railway. If one fails, the signalling system may show that a section of track is occupied even when there isn’t a train there. This means signals protecting that section will remain at red and trains cannot proceed normally.
Trains may still be able to run, but drivers will need to stop before the affected section and request verbal permission from the signaller before continuing past the red signal. They must then travel at a reduced speed so they can stop safely should they see anything ahead of them.
This takes longer than usual and can cause trains to queue behind one another. In severe cases, services may need to be cancelled, revised or diverted to prevent delays from building up across the wider network.
Network Rail signalling specialists are investigating the fault and will work to repair the affected equipment. Once the fault has been fixed and the signalling system is working normally, trains will be able to run at normal speeds again and the scheduled service can begin to recover.

nrIncident.routes: between Streatham Hill and Norwood Junction
nrIncident.message:
A fault with the signalling system between Streatham Hill and Norwood Junction means fewer lines are able to run on the line towards Crystal Palace. As a result, some trains between these stations will be cancelled or delayed by up to 15 minutes.
Disruption is expected until 14:00.
Customer advice:
Fewer trains than normal are able to run between Streatham Hill and Norwood Junction. This is due to a signal failure in the Crystal Palace area.
Services that normally run between London Victoria and West Croydon via Crystal Palace will divert via Streatham Common instead. This is only affecting South-bound trains. Trains towards London will run as booked.
If you require the following stations you will need to change at West Croydon for London-bound connections:
• Streatham Hill
• West Norwood
• Gipsy Hill
• Crystal Palace
• Norwood Junction
Make sure you leave to least an additional 15 minutes to complete your journey.
Please ensure to check before you travel using our online journey planners and live departure boards for the latest information.
Planning your journey:
For help planning your journey, check live departure boards, view a live network map or see alternative route guides.
If you’re travelling within London, you can use the TfL Journey Planner.
Stay up to date on the move with Southern’s WhatsApp channel. Live updates are available Monday to Friday, 07:00–21:00.
Can you tell me more about the incident?
Track circuits are part of the signalling system and are used to detect where trains are on the railway. If one fails, the signalling system may show that a section of track is occupied even when there isn’t a train there. This means signals protecting that section will remain at red and trains cannot proceed normally.
Trains may still be able to run, but drivers will need to stop before the affected section and request verbal permission from the signaller before continuing past the red signal. They must then travel at a reduced speed so they can stop safely should they see anything ahead of them.
This takes longer than usual and can cause trains to queue behind one another. In severe cases, services may need to be cancelled, revised or diverted to prevent delays from building up across the wider network.
Network Rail signalling specialists are investigating the fault and will work to repair the affected equipment. Once the fault has been fixed and the signalling system is working normally, trains will be able to run at normal speeds again and the scheduled service can begin to recover.
